extracted.intended_audience: vehicle owners/consumers concerned about unintended acceleration and potential class-action plaintiffs (and people researching Toyota acceleration defects)
extracted.subtask_description: A news-style consumer-facing article explaining what unintended (unexpected) vehicle acceleration is, possible causes, what to do during an event, industry/regulatory responses, and criteria for pursuing legal action or joining a class-action investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and causes of unexpected acceleration
rubrics_metrics.description: If a vehicle accelerates unexpectedly, it can put drivers, passengers, or even pedestrians at risk for a potentially deadly collision. There may be several causes of unexpected acceleration in vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations from NHTSA and other agencies have found that driver error may contribute, but vehicle issues can also cause unexpected acceleration. Examples given: multiple or bulky floor mats that can slide onto the accelerator pedal; throttle linkages or throttle plates which stick together; accelerator getting stuck partially pushed down; possible electrical system defects. Use these categories when diagnosing or describing an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency steps to take during accidental/unexpected acceleration
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate recommended actions if experiencing accidental acceleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the engine on to retain power brakes and power steering; brake hard on the brake pedal — do not push the acceleration pedal; put the transmission in neutral or depress the clutch; only use emergency brakes if the service brakes have failed (apply gently to avoid spin or rollover); maneuver the car to a safe spot as it slows, stop safely, then shut off the engine; put the car in park and exit the vehicle. (Presented as a step-by-step emergency procedure.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented/commonly-reported causes specific to Toyota incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported causes and theories behind the Toyota acceleration reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports since 2009 led to recalls in 2009–2010 for sticky pedals and sliding floor mats (floor mats could slide onto the accelerator). Some consumers and reports argued electrical/system-level issues or the accelerator getting stuck partially depressed. Note Toyota denied some electrical-defect assertions. When evaluating Toyota incidents, consider recalls, sticky pedals, floor mats, and potential electrical/throttle-mechanism defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of corporate/regulatory consequences and liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Events and outcomes that indicate manufacturer accountability or regulatory action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: federal criminal probe (FBI argued Toyota concealed issues), large settlement with federal prosecutors (March 2014 $1.2 billion agreement requiring Toyota to admit it 'misled U.S. consumers' about safety issues), hundreds of private settlements (e.g., 537 legal claims settled since 2014), high settlement rates in MDL (97% settled in one document). Use recalls, criminal investigations, large fines/settlements, and private claim settlements as signals of corporate consequences and possible liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry and regulatory responses / safety-technology considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: How regulators and manufacturers have considered or implemented technical fixes to address unintended acceleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA explored requiring a brake-override system that would override throttle if the driver slammed the brake; the proposal did not become mandatory because manufacturers implemented their own safety systems. Consumer Reports data showing over 40% of sudden-acceleration complaints involve Toyota vehicles is cited. When assessing risk or a vehicle's safety, check whether override/brake-override or other fail-safe safety systems are present and whether manufacturers have taken voluntary steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to do if you suspect your vehicle is defective
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer actions to take when suspecting a safety defect in a vehicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check with the vehicle manufacturer to see if a recall has been issued. If not, report the issue to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) on their website. Note: over the last half-century NHTSA has recalled more than 390 million vehicles. If a safety defect places you or loved ones in danger, you may be able to file a lawsuit to pursue compensation; consult an attorney for case-specific advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for qualifying for a class action lawsuit investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed eligibility conditions for joining a vehicle safety class action investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may qualify if any of the following apply: your vehicle has a safety defect that has not been included in a recall; you or someone you love has been injured in a vehicle with a safety defect (even if that vehicle was already included in a recall); your vehicle has a safety defect but is no longer in the warranty period; OR your vehicle has a safety defect that should be covered under the warranty but isn’t. Guidance also recommends consulting an experienced attorney (the site offers free case evaluations/connects to attorneys) to determine claim viability and navigate litigation.
